lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Pollux, I have an errand for you. As soon as you get upstairs—it’s your turn to come back to life tomorrow, isn't it?—if you happen to see Menippus the Cynic anywhere... You’ll probably find him in Corinth by the Craneion, or in the Lyceum, laughing at the philosophers arguing with each other. Tell him this.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: "Diogenes says, Menippus, if you’ve laughed enough at the world up there, come down here to laugh a lot more. Up there, your laughter always had an edge of doubt—there was a lot of 'who really knows what happens after death?' But down here you can laugh with absolute certainty, just like I do. Especially when you see the rich, the satraps, and the tyrants reduced to such absolute nobodies that you can only tell them apart by their crying—and you realize how completely soft and unmanly they are when they remember the world above."

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell him that. And tell him to pack his satchel full of lupin seeds. And if he happens to find a crossroads offering to Hecate on his way, or a purification egg, to bring that too.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: I’ll tell him, Diogenes. But just so I’m sure—what does he look like?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Old. Bald. Wears a battered little cloak with so many holes it's basically all doors, open to every wind and patched together with random rags. He’s always laughing, and he's usually mocking those pompous philosophers.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Would you like me to give you a message for the philosophers themselves, while we’re at it?

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Go ahead. It won't weigh me down.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell them, generally speaking, to stop talking nonsense. Stop arguing about the nature of the universe, stop planting horns on each other, stop building crocodiles, and stop teaching people to waste their minds on impossible riddles.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: But if I criticize their wisdom, they'll just tell me I'm an ignorant, uneducated meathead.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell them, from me, to go to hell.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: [chuckles] I’ll deliver that one too, Diogenes.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the rich, my dearest little Pollux, deliver this message from us: "Why, you idiots, do you hoard your gold? Why torture yourselves calculating interest and piling millions upon millions, when you're going to show up here any minute with exactly one obol to your name?"

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: I will tell them that too.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And the handsome and the athletic. Megillus of Corinth and Damoxenus the wrestler. Tell them that down here there is no blonde hair, no sparkling eyes, no dark eyes, no rosy cheeks. No tight sinews, no broad shoulders. Down here it's all just one pile of dust, as the saying goes. Bare skulls, completely stripped of beauty.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Not hard to say that to the handsome and athletic, either.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the poor, my Spartan friend—there are plenty of them, miserable and crying about their poverty. Tell them to stop weeping and wailing. Explain the complete equality we have down here. Tell them they’ll see the rich from up there looking absolutely no better than they do. Oh, and your fellow Spartans—if you don’t mind—rebuke them from me. Tell them they’ve gone soft.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Not a word about the Spartans, Diogenes. [pause] I won't have it. But what you said for the others, I will deliver.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: We’ll leave them be, since you prefer. Just take the other messages.
